pages.text: Lights!
pages.title: Lights!

pages.text:
Read and make this together.

Before you start, use the separate helper guide to prepare the exact parts and check the build.

A picture shows an idea. It does not show every wire.

Physical kit testing is still pending.
pages.title: For your grown-up

pages.text:
The tent has a door.
The tent has a bed.
Now it needs a light.
pages.title: A light for the tent

pages.text:
Can a light shine
if there is a gap
in one of its wires?

Your helper adds a resistor.
It helps protect the little light.
With the battery unplugged,
build the wire loop together.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Prepare a known-good 3 V loop, confirm breadboard strip continuity, mark trimmed LED polarity, and keep a spare red LED and matched AA pair. Do not plant a short circuit.

pages.text:
Your helper checks the loop.
Plug in the battery.
Does the light shine?
Unplug before your helper opens one wire.
Check together, then try again.

A gap breaks the path.
Our light goes out.
Unplug before closing the gap.
Check the loop and try once more.

Where will your light go?
In a cave?
In a tiny house?
Tell someone what made it go dark.

This flap has a secret.
Close it,
and a little light can shine.
pages.title: The secret flap

pages.text:
What do you think happens
when the shiny foil pieces
stop touching?

Unplug the battery.
Make the flap with your helper.
The two foil pieces must meet
when the flap closes.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Prepare foil with smooth edges and secure insulated joints. Keep the entire switch in the return path. No foil across battery terminals.

pages.text:
Ask your helper to check.
Connect the battery.
Open the flap. Close it.
Open it again.
What does the light do?

Touching foil closes the path.
The light comes on.
A gap opens the path.
The light goes off.

Can you make a paper door
that works the same way?
Tell someone where the path breaks.

Here is a paperclip.
Here is a plastic lid.
They look different.
Will they do different things?
pages.title: The paperclip test

pages.text:
Which one could help
our little light shine?
What is your guess?

Your helper makes a safe tester.
It has one gap.
With the battery unplugged,
put one clean, dry object in the gap.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Approve clean dry samples in advance. Never test skin, sockets, battery terminals, liquids, sharp scraps or dismantled appliances.

pages.text:
Ask your helper to check.
Connect the battery and look.
Unplug before trying the next object.
Try four objects.
Which ones make the light shine?

Metal lets electricity pass.
It is a conductor.
Plastic often does not.
Check for loose wires
before deciding.

Choose a safe mystery object
for your helper to test.
What made you think
it would work?

An LED is a tiny light.
This one has two legs.
Does it matter
which way they go?
pages.title: Turn it around

pages.text:
If we turn the LED around,
will it still shine?

Unplug the battery.
Ask your helper to mark the legs.
Build the loop together.
Keep the resistor in its place.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Use only the reviewed 3 V red-LED kit. Verify polarity markings and reverse tolerance for the actual selected component.

pages.text:
Check together, then try it.
Unplug.
Your helper turns only the LED around.
Check again before connecting power.
What changed?

An LED has a direction.
In our loop, one way shines.
The other way stays dark.
The resistor stays in place.

Make a little paper label
to show the right way round.
How could you help someone
remember it?

Our little house
has two windows.
We want a light
in each one.
pages.title: Two bright windows

pages.text:
If one light loses its path,
must the other go dark too?

Unplug the battery.
Build two paths with your helper.
Each light needs
its own resistor.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Prepare two matched ordinary red LEDs. No single shared resistor for two parallel LEDs. Use branch labels instead of depending on wire colors.

pages.text:
Check together, then connect power.
Look at both lights.
Unplug before your helper opens one path.
Check and try again.
Does the other light stay on?

Each light has its own path.
One path can break
while the other stays whole.

Make two rooms for your lights.
Show someone each path.
What do both paths share?

A house in the woods.
A star in the sky.
What picture could you make
with one little light?
pages.title: A glowing picture

pages.text:
Where should your light go
so someone can see
what you made?

Draw your picture first.
Keep the battery unplugged
while you and your helper
fit the little light and wires.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Prerequisites include C01, C02 and C04. Require C05 readiness before an optional second branch. Precut windows and keep cells accessible.

pages.text:
Your helper checks the wires.
Turn on the light.
Move the picture gently
to its display spot.
Does it still work?

Paper can tug on a wire.
A wire can come loose.
Unplug before fixing it.
Then check and try again.

Change one part of your picture.
What looks better now?
Show someone what you changed.

books.title: Tell a light what to do

pages.text: Tell a light what to do
pages.title: Tell a light what to do

pages.text:
Read and make this together.

Before you start, use the separate helper guide to prepare the exact parts and check the build.

A picture shows an idea. It does not show every wire.

Physical kit testing is still pending.
pages.title: For your grown-up

pages.text:
The board has a tiny light.
On. Off.
On. Off.
Can we change its blink?
pages.title: Blink, little light

pages.text:
What will happen
if the light waits
for less time?

Your helper opens the code.
Find both waits marked 500.
Watch the first blink pattern
before changing anything.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Prepare IDE, board package and USB access before the learner session. No wiring needed and no external LED resistor needed for the onboard L LED.

pages.text:
Change both waits to 250.
Ask your helper to upload.
Watch the same little light.
Is it faster now?

The code repeats.
Turn on. Wait.
Turn off. Wait.
Shorter waits make faster blinks.

Make a blink pattern of your own.
Can someone recognize it?
Tell them which waits you changed.

Red. Green. Yellow.
Our tiny town
needs a traffic light.
pages.title: The little traffic light

pages.text:
If green stays on longer,
will the whole pattern
take longer too?

Keep USB unplugged.
Build the three lights
with your helper.
Each light gets its own resistor.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Use ordinary low-current indicator LEDs. Confirm each chosen color lights acceptably on the reviewed Uno/220 ohm branch.

pages.text:
Ask your helper to check and upload.
Watch one whole pattern.
Now make only the green wait
twice as long.
Watch again.

The order can stay the same
while the timing changes.
A longer green wait
makes this whole pattern longer.

How long should red last
in your pretend town?
Choose a time, try it,
and tell someone what changed.

Press the button.
The light comes on.
Let go.
The light goes off.
pages.title: The button knows

pages.text:
How does the board know
when your finger
has pressed the button?

Unplug USB.
Your helper shows you
the two switch contacts.
Build the checked button-and-light circuit together.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Prepare IDE/Uno support offline where possible. Verify the exact switch model, LED polarity and data cable. Do the wiring unpowered. Keep a printed HIGH/LOW observation option for learners who cannot use Serial independently.

pages.text:
Ask your helper to check and upload.
Press. Let go.
Try five times.
Look at the light
and the words on the screen.

Our button reads LOW
when you press it.
The code uses that LOW
to turn the light on.

Can a paper flap
press your button for you?
Unplug before changing the build.
Show someone how your flap works.

One light.
Two different glows.
How can we make
the light look dimmer?
pages.title: A softer glow

pages.text:
Which number will look brighter:
64 or 192?

Unplug the board.
Build the light and resistor
with your helper.
Let them choose the right connection.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Keep the LED away from eyes and use the fixed resistor. Do not present PWM as a variable DC power supply.

pages.text:
Ask your helper to check and upload.
Try 64.
Then try 192.
Watch from the same place.
Which glow looks brighter?

The light flashes too fast to see.
More time on
usually looks brighter.
Less time on looks dimmer.

Can you make a slow, soft glow
for a paper lighthouse?
Tell someone what the number changes.

Two short flashes.
One long flash.
Someone at the pretend camp
is sending a message.
pages.title: A secret message

pages.text:
Could you tell two messages apart
just by watching
how long the light stays on?

Choose a silent light pattern
with your helper.
A quiet beep works too.
Let your helper check the sound first.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Adult approves current rating and comfortable sound level before class. No sound is required. Built-in LED alternative requires no external LED wiring.

pages.text:
Try one short signal
and one long signal.
Keep the sound comfortable,
or use only light.
Ask someone to copy the pattern.

A signal can be short or long.
Our light uses that length
to make a message.

Make two secret messages.
Can a partner tell them apart
three times in a row?

Your finger is ready.
The light is not.
Wait...
Wait...
pages.title: Wait for the light

pages.text:
If you press before the light,
should that try count?

Unplug USB.
Build the button and light
with your helper.
Ask them to check and upload the game.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Explain timing limitations. Pseudorandom delays and 20 ms debounce support the lesson but do not produce certified human reaction measurements.

pages.text:
Let go of the button.
Wait for the light.
Then press!
Try an early press once too.
What does the game say?

The game checks
when you press.
An early press is a false start.
A press after the light gives a time.

Try five fair turns.
What changes as you practise?
Your helper can explain
why the timing is only an estimate.
Cardboard on the move
pages.title: Cardboard on the move

pages.text:
Read and make this together.

Before you start, use the separate helper guide to prepare the exact parts and check the build.

A picture shows an idea. It does not show every wire.

Physical kit testing is still pending.
pages.title: For your grown-up

pages.text:
This cardboard jaw
has a long, long tail.
Push the tail down.
What could rise?
pages.title: The cardboard jaw

pages.text:
Where would you push
to lift the same paper load
more easily?

Your helper fits the turning point.
It is called a pivot.
Tape on a tiny paper load.
Find the two marked push spots.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Precut and punch holes out of the child activity; no knives or sharp punches in learner steps. Dry-run clearance and protect paper-fastener prongs. Choose a very light load and accept inconclusive effort judgments.

pages.text:
Push gently at the near spot.
Then try the far spot.
Lift to the same mark each time.
Keep fingers away from the pivot.

The far spot can feel easier.
But your hand moves farther
to lift the load
the same height.

Turn your lever into an animal.
What moves when you push?
Show someone the easier push spot.

A handle turns.
The marker moves.
A line grows
across the paper.
pages.title: The drawing machine

pages.text:
If we move one pivot,
will the line
follow the same path?

Your helper fits the paper pins.
Tape on a light marker.
The parts must turn freely.
Never force them.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Bench-check this exact four-bar geometry and alternate hole before learners use it. Adult does all piercing and fastener fitting. Use limited hand motion, no motors.

pages.text:
Turn the handle through
the same small move three times.
Stop. Your helper moves one pivot.
Try the same move again.

The links guide each other.
A new pivot spot
can make a new path.

Turn your lines into a picture.
Which pivot did you move?
Tell someone how the line changed.

Our paper leaf
wants to wave hello.
Can a little motor help?
pages.title: A leaf that waves

pages.text:
Will two different commands
make the leaf point
two different ways?

This small motor is a servo.
Your helper sets up its own power
and checks it without the leaf.
Keep hands clear.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Use a guarded low-force micro-servo. Adult prepares the regulated supply and handles both-source isolation. Verify startup motion before attaching the arm.

pages.text:
Turn both power sources off.
Your helper fits the light paper leaf.
After another check, watch it move
between the two safe positions.

The board sends a signal.
The servo tries to turn
to the position we asked for.

Change a pause in the code
with your helper.
Can your leaf wave slowly?
Keep the same safe positions.

A little turn here.
A little move there.
Can your dial
move a paper puppet?
pages.title: Turn the dial

pages.text:
What will the puppet do
when you turn the dial
toward its other end?

Your helper sets up
the dial and servo.
The servo keeps its own power supply.
All wiring changes happen with power off.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Use a real three-terminal 10 kohm potentiometer and check its pinout. Do not extend servo limits to make a dial appear more responsive.

pages.text:
Turn slowly.
Try the low end,
the middle and the high end.
Keep clear of the moving arm.

The dial changes a reading.
The code uses that reading
to choose a servo position.

Give your puppet a job.
Can it point to three places?
Show someone how the dial
controls the move.

A paper boat is coming.
The bridge is in the way.
Up, little bridge!
pages.title: Up goes the bridge

pages.text:
Could a button
lift the bridge
without your hand touching it?

Your helper checks the servo first.
With both power sources off,
fit the light bridge together.
Leave the hinge clear.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Prebuild and guard the hinge and linkage. Adult tests startup, both targets and clearances before student interaction.

pages.text:
After your helper checks,
press and let go.
Watch the bridge open and close.
Stop if it catches or strains.

The button sends a request.
The code picks a position.
The servo moves the bridge.

Make a paper boat
that fits your river.
What would you check
if the bridge got stuck?

This paper creature
has something to say.
No words.
Just a wiggle.
pages.title: A creature with a wiggle

pages.text:
Could a slow move
and a quick move
look like different moods?

Your helper checks the servo
with nothing attached.
Turn both power sources off
before fitting your light paper creature.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Keep audience feedback anonymous and local. Use the reviewed servo setup and avoid claiming a particular gesture objectively means an emotion.

pages.text:
After your helper checks,
watch the two moves.
Change one pause in the code.
Keep the same safe positions.

Timing can change
how a move looks.
Your partner might see excitement.
You might see surprise.

Give your creature a greeting.
What did your partner think
it was saying?
What can a sensor tell?
pages.title: What can a sensor tell?

pages.text:
Read and make this together.

Before you start, use the separate helper guide to prepare the exact parts and check the build.

A picture shows an idea. It does not show every wire.

Physical kit testing is still pending.
pages.title: For your grown-up

pages.text:
A paper cloud
passes over the sensor.
Will the board
notice the shade?
pages.title: A paper cloud

pages.text:
Will the number get bigger
or smaller
when you cover the sensor?

Your helper builds and checks
the light-sensor circuit.
Ask them to show you
the changing numbers.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Use a two-lead LDR, not a module. Verify actual resistor value and divider direction. Prepare Serial display or have the mentor read values aloud; learners can sort high/low cards instead of typing.

pages.text:
Watch three numbers in room light.
Shade the sensor with dry card.
Watch three more.
Take the card away.
What happens now?

For our circuit,
brighter light usually gives
a bigger number.
Shade usually gives a smaller one.

Make a paper cloud
that can slide past the sensor.
Tell someone what happened
to the numbers.

The little reading nook
is getting dark.
Can its lamp
turn on by itself?
pages.title: A light for the dark

pages.text:
How could the board decide
when it is
dark enough?

Your helper checks the sensor and LED.
Read the numbers in light and shade.
Together, choose a number
between those two groups.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Use local recorded calibration. The sample 500 threshold is an editable starting value, not a promised universal setting.

pages.text:
Try the light rule.
Cover the sensor.
Uncover it.
What happens to the lamp?
Now try a different room.

That number tells our code
when to turn the lamp on.
In another room,
we may need a new number.

Make a paper shade
for your reading nook.
Did the lamp ever turn on
when you did not expect it?

Hello, cardboard wall!
The sensor sends out sound.
Will an echo
come back?
pages.title: An echo in a box

pages.text:
Will a closer wall
send the echo back
sooner?

Your helper builds and checks
the sound sensor.
Hold a flat cardboard target
facing its two round openings.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Confirm exact module pinout. ECHO is a 5 V signal and needs a separately reviewed level-shifting variant for 3.3 V boards.

pages.text:
Try about 10, 20 and 40 centimetres.
Read three numbers at each spot.
If no reading comes back,
write “missing,” not zero.

Sound goes to the wall
and back again.
A longer trip
usually takes more time.

Try a soft fabric target
at the same safe distance.
Does it give the same clear echo?

Our toy block
is rolling toward the wall.
Can a little light
give us a clue?
pages.title: Getting closer

pages.text:
As the block gets closer,
should the flashes get
faster or slower?

Your helper checks
the sensor and flashing light.
This is a tabletop model,
not a safety device.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Never present this as automotive safety equipment. The invalid-reading state must remain visible in Serial; an off LED alone cannot mean safe.

pages.text:
Try the target at
15, 35 and 70 centimetres.
Count flashes for the same time.
Then remove the target.
What does the screen say?

Closer readings make faster flashes.
A missing echo means
we do not know the distance.
An off light cannot mean “all clear.”

Can you invent a different sign
for “I do not know”?
Tell someone why
your model needs it.

Here is a tiny bead.
Your hand is warm.
Could the bead
notice?
pages.title: A warm little bead

pages.text:
What might happen
to the number
when the bead gets warmer?

Your helper checks
the insulated bead and its wires.
Touch only the dry, covered bead.
Keep fingers off the metal legs.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Use a documented insulated bead. No contact with exposed leads. No flame, hot water, heater, calibrated temperature or medical claims.

pages.text:
Watch the room readings.
Gently warm the checked bead
with dry fingertips.
Let go and wait.
Watch the numbers again.

The numbers may change slowly.
They are clues about this bead.
They are not yet
a temperature in degrees.

Draw the way
your numbers changed.
If the change was too small to tell,
say so.

The treasure box opens.
Light slips inside.
Can our sensor
spot the change?
pages.title: The open box

pages.text:
Would opening the box
always make it brighter
inside?

Your helper checks
the light sensor and lamp.
Keep wires clear of the lid.
Compare open and closed readings.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Keep cardboard dry and wires unpinched. No personal valuables or security promises. Optional public sharing stays disabled.

pages.text:
Try five openings
in one room.
Use the same rule
in a darker room.
Does it still notice every opening?

The sensor follows light,
not the lid itself.
A dark room
can hide the clue.

Move the sensor
with power off and your helper’s help.
Check and try again.
Did the new spot work better?
I made that!
pages.title: I made that!

pages.text:
Read and make this together.

Before you start, use the separate helper guide to prepare the exact parts and check the build.

A picture shows an idea. It does not show every wire.

Physical kit testing is still pending.
pages.title: For your grown-up

pages.text:
There is something
inside this box.
All we can see
is a little tab.
pages.title: What is in the box?

pages.text:
If you push the tab
and let go,
will it come back?

Your helper gives you
a safe cardboard mystery box.
Look at the outside first.
Leave the inside closed.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Adult builds and tests the contained mechanism. Use no hazardous appliance, strong spring, powered motor or loose snap-back part. Any internal reveal is adult-controlled.

pages.text:
Push gently and let go.
Try the same move again.
What did you see?
What might be making it happen?

“The tab came back”
is something we saw.
“An elastic band pulled it”
is one possible reason.

Think of another reason.
What gentle test could help?
Ask before opening the box.

The little light
will not shine.
Welcome to
the repair shop.
pages.title: The light is out

pages.text:
Could a loose wire
and a backwards LED
both make the light go dark?

Your helper has hidden
one safe problem in a checked circuit.
Unplug the battery.
Look before changing anything.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Before learners arrive, verify known-good operation and log it. Disconnect power; plant exactly one: open return lead, reversed red LED, or disconnected resistor lead. Never plant shorts, overheating, excess voltage, resistor bypass or damaged cells. Seal the fault record until debrief.

pages.text:
Choose one thing to check.
Let your helper check the change.
Then try power.
Unplug before trying another fix.

One small change
can give us a useful clue.
Changing everything at once
hides which part helped.

Tell your repair story.
What did you check?
What happened?
What would you try next?

This machine makes
a lovely little move.
Could yours do that
with different cardboard parts?
pages.title: Copy the move

pages.text:
If one link gets longer,
will the end
move the same way?

Watch the cardboard model move.
Draw what it does.
Your helper fits your paper pins
and checks that the parts turn freely.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Use M01/M02 readiness and precut parts. No powered reverse engineering, sharp tools or high-force mechanism.

pages.text:
Try the same small handle move
three times.
Stop before moving one paper strip
or its turning point.
Try again. What changed?

Different parts
can make similar moves.
But one version may wobble
more than the other.

Choose one thing
you want to make better.
Try one change.
Did it help?

One paper flap.
Two handles.
Which would you
like to use?
pages.title: Two handles

pages.text:
Would the same handle
feel easiest
to everyone?

Imagine someone using your flap.
Would they pull it or push it?
Make two paper handles
with your helper.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. No medical claims or disability simulation. No names or health histories. Use voluntary comfortable partner testing and only preapproved paper mechanisms.

pages.text:
Ask a partner to try them
in a comfortable way.
Listen to what they say.
Change one handle and try again.

A bigger grip
might help one person.
Another person
might choose a different shape.

Show both versions.
What did your partner
help you notice?

This paper flag
keeps falling over.
What could help
it stand?
pages.title: One more try

pages.text:
Which part should we test first:
the wobbly base
or the decoration?

Choose your six craft materials
with your helper.
Say what your model must do.
Make a quick first version.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. Use the default no-electronics route for this complete manuscript. Additional electrical versions need their own source, prerequisites and review. Adult preps holes and fasteners.

pages.text:
Try it.
What falls, bends or slips?
Change just one part.
Try the same test
with your second version.

The first try
told us what needed work.
Now we have
something useful to change.

Show both versions.
Which change helped?
What would you try
with one less material?

Look what you made!
A little house.
A wiggly creature.
Something that began as an idea.
pages.title: I made that!

pages.text:
What could you show
to help someone understand
how it works?

Ask your helper to check your model.
You can show a drawing instead.
Find your notes.
Keep names and private details off the display.
pages.helper_note: Use the full helper guide for this lesson. Do not improvise wiring from an illustration. No publishing requirement. Adult checks the demonstration and any media. Keep feedback respectful, voluntary and local.

pages.text:
Tell someone:
“This was my first idea.
This is what happened.
This is what I changed.”

A story about a mistake
can help explain
a better idea.

Ask your listener
what they noticed.
What would you like
to make next?
